title: Caron and the Melody of the Drip
markdown:
Caron Buttonwood, a weasel with a heart as warm as sun on old parchment, surveyed the Grand Whispering Library. To most it was a place of quiet reverence. To Caron it was a concert hall, and he its most dignified conductor. Today the hall had acoustics. A persistent drip marked its territory on a pile of forgotten dictionaries. He adjusted the spectacles on his nose. He led the Library Chorus, and perfection was the goal, even if the stage was a little damp. Old paper usually smelled like comfort. Now a faint earthy plaster joined it. He imagined a hushed audience, then the jarring plink of water on polished floor. It would not do.

Dignity, he believed, was a performance you put on with care. Theo the fox, boundless and full of odd news, often said, "Caron, you fret too much. Just sing." Caron knew better. Dignity was oak. It was the difference between a maestro and a busker.

Then a thick envelope arrived, stamped Official Library Protocols for Public Performances. Whiskers twitched. He unfolded stiff paper. The crisp sound argued with the damp air. Requirement 7B: performers must execute a Subtle Salutation of the Sunbeams, a precisely angled head tilt and a slow three-part knee bend, while humming a note of exactly G-flat. Caron blinked behind his spectacles. G-flat? His music lived in joyful C majors and soaring A minors. The rules made a pretzel look honest. Requirement 14C: all vocal exercises must incorporate the Wobbly Whistle of Welcome, escalating and de-escalating warbles designed to disarm potential grumblers. A tremor went through his chest, like a bassoon finding a draught. This was not dignity. This was a grand piano balanced on a teacup.

Should he, renowned for a smooth baritone and an elegant stance, attempt such silliness? He pictured the G-flat cracking, knees folding like a badly made swan. Tradition pressed. He decided, with a flicker in the eye, that he must. He would prove the protocols held a hidden sense. Perhaps G-flat was the secret of depth, and the whistle the key to hearts.

Theo arrived that afternoon, tail wagging like a metronome with opinions, damp prints on the polish. "Ready to practice, Maestro? I brought a sort of musical umbrella." He unfurled a tattered flowered thing, petals faded and curling. "In case the sky joins in."

Caron, already attempting the Salutation, wobbled. Spectacles slid. "Theo, this is solemn artistic integrity, not weather preparedness. And please, try not to splash."

Theo grinned, white teeth in a foxy face.

Rehearsals would have made a slapstick comic weep with joy. Caron’s Wobbly Whistle sounded less like welcome and more like a leaky tap impersonating a startled goose. Theo joined in, a duet of squeaks that sent dust bunnies scattering. Then came the greeting for Madame Grimshaw, the visiting badger, a critic of stern looks and sterner words. Caron’s three-part knee bend was so slow Theo whispered, "Are you asleep? Shall I wake you with a gentle nip?"

The dripping worsened. A large drop landed on the sheet music and smudged a crescendo. Caron grabbed a stack of encyclopedias and balanced them on his head to shield the notes. The sight of a weasel under a tower of books, face a mask of concentration, surprised a snort from Theo, quickly muffled by Caron’s paw as he tried to stay regal.

One grey afternoon, between rehearsals, they sat under the leak and did not practice. The drip kept its own time. Dust hung in a slant of window-light. Theo held the umbrella shut and, for once, did not invent news. Caron listened until the dictionaries sounded almost like a section he had forgotten to write parts for, a wet metronome no protocol had mentioned.

The day of the Hymns of the High Shelves dawned grey and damp. The air held anticipation and a hint of mildew. Madame Grimshaw sat in the front row, nose nearly on the stage, expression as unyielding as an unread manuscript. Bookworms rustled. Then the leak performed its solo. A steady stream cascaded from a crack in the plaster, directly onto the Chorus’s mark. A gasp moved the crowd. Caron’s composure frayed. Whiskers drooped. The masterpiece was being washed off the floor.

Madame Grimshaw’s brow furrowed. A murmur of worried pages. He had tried so hard to be oak, and the roof was reminding him he was a weasel in a wet library.

Theo sidled close, a warm nudge at the elbow. "Caron," he whispered, "they love your singing. Not your dripping. And that leak has a rather interesting rhythm."

Caron looked at Theo, at the hypnotic stream, at faces concerned and amused and waiting. A single clear note formed. The protocols were ridiculous. Unshakeable dignity was a handkerchief against a river. The music was real. It came from the chest, not the envelope.

He straightened his spectacles. He walked into the splash, cool on his paws. He breathed, and instead of G-flat he hummed an unburdened C major, bright as a break in cloud. He skipped the knee bends and the whistle. He pulled out Theo’s flowered umbrella and held it aloft, faded petals suddenly defiant. From beneath his waistcoat he produced a small gleaming bucket, a secret kept for just-in-case, and set it under the most vigorous drip. He did not ignore the water. He sang the quiet corners, the stories in the walls, and, with a glint, the Melody of the Drip, Drip, Drip. He invented a jaunty line about a weasel who found his voice in a rainy afternoon, laughter mixed with patter. The umbrella swayed. The bucket worked. For the first time that day he felt, gloriously, like himself.

The audience smiled, then laughed, a bright ripple in the cool spray and the dusty-sweet air. Then they cheered. Madame Grimshaw’s sternness remembered how to soften; her foot found the beat. When the watery ode ended, they stood. Applause mingled with the cheerful plink in the bucket. Caron bowed, not to protocol, but with a joyful sweep of tail, umbrella still overhead, bucket catching every last drop.
characters: Caron (kind-hearted weasel choir leader), Theo (fox friend), Madame Grimshaw (stern visiting critic)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing story for older children
